questions.question: Why use `next/dynamic` to import a heavy client library like a rich text editor?
options: It makes the library's own code execute faster
It splits the library into a separate JS chunk that only downloads once the component actually renders, instead of bloating the initial page load
It converts the library into a Server Component automatically
It is required for all third-party npm packages
questions.explanation: `next/dynamic` defers loading a component's code until it's actually needed, keeping it out of the initial bundle for users who never trigger it.

questions.question: When should you pass `ssr: false` to `next/dynamic`?
options: Always, for every dynamically imported component
For libraries that touch `window`/`document` at module scope and would crash if rendered on the server
questions.explanation: `ssr: false` skips server rendering entirely for components that assume a browser environment is already present at import time.

questions.question: What does `@next/bundle-analyzer` help you find?
options: An interactive treemap of each route's JS, useful for spotting accidentally-imported heavy dependencies
questions.explanation: It visualizes what's actually inside each route's bundle, making it easy to spot something like an entire icon library imported for one icon.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is the single biggest performance lever in a Next.js app?
options: Server Components by default — most of a typical page ships zero JS for content that never needed to be interactive
questions.explanation: Because Server Components don't ship their code to the client at all, defaulting to them removes far more JS than any later optimization step.
